title: Food and hosting
verifiedBy: Claude Opus 5 — LLM review, authorised by repo owner

rules.text: ēst AGAINST est, AND THIS MODULE IS WHERE THE MACRON PAYS FOR ITSELF. ēst is 'he eats' and est is 'he is', and the only difference between them is the length of the e. L1-M1 took est for 'is' and every module since was forbidden to write ēst so this one could have it. Pānem est is a grammatical Latin sentence meaning 'he is bread' — nothing fails, nothing looks wrong, and the reader is simply told something else.

edō IS IRREGULAR AND IS LEARNED AS A SET: edō 'I eat', ēst 'he eats', ēs 'eat!', edere 'to eat'. It has a second infinitive, one bar from esse ('to be'), and this course names it in prose and writes it nowhere — edere is the infinitive used here. One verb generating three near-collisions with the commonest verb in the language is a fact about Latin rather than a decision of this course, and the only defence is to write every mark.

ēs AGAINST es is the same trade one row further down: ēs is 'eat!' and es is 'you are'. Two of the module's four collisions come out of the same verb, and both are resolved by length alone. When you read Latin without macrons — which is most printed Latin — these are the sentences you work out from context.

HOSTING IN LATIN IS IMPERATIVES, WARMLY MEANT: bibe ('drink!'), ēs ('eat!'), and L1-M8's dā, with M1's quaesō available to soften any of them. There is no natural Latin for 'would you like…?' — a host gives an order and it reads as generosity. An English speaker hears a bare imperative as brusque and will want to build a question; there is nothing to build it out of.

REFUSING WITHOUT OFFENCE, in three phrases and no constructions: nōlō, grātiās ('no thanks'), satis est ('that is enough'), and benignē — which is the trap. benignē means 'kindly' and is a REFUSAL: it declines an offer by praising it. An English speaker who says it meaning 'how kind of you!' has just said no, and been understood.

THE ENCLITIC -que, BACK FROM L1-M10 AND EARNING ITS PLACE: vīnum aquam-que volō. It rides on the back of the SECOND thing joined, never the first, and this course writes the hyphen so the seam is visible where Latin writes aquamque. et is equally correct and flatter; -que ties two things into one request.

words.note: 'Bread': pānis as the subject, pānem as the thing eaten. L1-M8's word, back as food rather than as something to buy.
'I eat', and irregular enough to learn whole: edō 'I eat', ēst 'he eats', edere 'to eat'. The bar on ēst is the only thing keeping it off the verb 'to be'.

sentences.trap: A plain sentence, and the last plain one in the module. edō looks regular and is not: the shapes this course writes are edō, ēst and edere, and learning them as a set now is cheaper than meeting ēst cold in the next sentence.

words.note: 'Drink!' — the order shape of L1-M5's bibō. Latin hosts with commands, warmly meant, and quaesō is how you take the edge off one.
'Water' as the object — aqua as the subject, aquam as the thing wanted or drunk. L1-M3's very first noun.
'Please', literally 'I beg'. M1's word, and it softens an order without changing it: the command stays a command.

sentences.trap: A bare order where English builds a question. 'Would you like some water?' has no natural Latin equivalent — a Roman host says 'drink!', and it is hospitality rather than rudeness. The instinct to soften it into a question is the thing to resist.

words.note: 'Dinner' — the one big meal of a Roman day, taken in the late afternoon. cēna as the subject, cēnam as the thing eaten.
'To eat' — edō's infinitive, and the one this course uses. The verb has a second infinitive, one bar from esse ('to be'), and this course never writes it.
'I want' — irregular, and the only verb for wanting: volō 'I want', vult 'he/she wants'. It takes an object or an infinitive.

sentences.trap: edere is edō's infinitive and it is not the only one. The other is a bar away from esse, 'to be' — the same collision as ēst and ēs, a third time, in the same verb. This course writes edere and leaves the other one alone, and the note says so rather than pretending it does not exist.
